title: Building Turbopuffer: Gergely Orosz (@pragmaticengineer ) × Simon Eskildsen (CEO)

primary.label: Retrieval, Search & Knowledge
primary.rationale: Turbopuffer is a vector search database built on S3 object storage. The technical core of the interview centers on retrieval infrastructure design: vector clustering, centroid-based search, S3 latency optimization for retrieval workloads, the cost economics of vector storage for search and recommendation systems, and the origin story driven by vector search cost problems at Readwise and Cursor. The inclusion criteria for retrieval_search_knowledge—'primary focus is retrieval, search, embeddings, or knowledge-base design for AI systems'—directly matches Turbopuffer's product and the discussion of its architecture.

secondary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
secondary.rationale: Turbopuffer serves as developer infrastructure that teams like Cursor and Readwise build their products on. The interview discusses platform adoption, customer integration workflows, the developer-facing cost model ($1/million vectors), and the hands-on technical support approach (debugging Postgres autovacuum) that built developer trust.

secondary.label: Inference & Model Systems
secondary.rationale: The interview covers CPU vs GPU tradeoffs (AVX 512, SIMD), cloud capacity constraints driven by RL and AI agent workloads, latency/cost optimization for compute-intensive search operations, and P99/P999 latency management. While not primarily about model serving, these systems-level compute and latency topics are significant secondary themes.

secondary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
secondary.rationale: Napkin math—computing theoretical performance ceilings from first-principles hardware numbers to challenge benchmarks—is a recurring methodology theme. Toxyroxy fault injection in CI represents systematic testing methodology that uncovered real driver-level bugs. Both are significant but not the primary focus of the current work discussed.

domains.label: Search & Knowledge
domains.rationale: Turbopuffer is a vector search engine serving retrieval use cases including code search (Cursor) and recommendation systems (Readwise). The domain directly matches the product's core function and the technical problems discussed.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Turbopuffer is infrastructure consumed by software builders; the interview discusses the platform's developer-facing API, cost model, integration experience, and the trust-building process with developer customers.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The interview covers broad engineering principles (napkin math, simplicity, self-education method), venture capital philosophy, and remote company culture that apply across domains beyond any single vertical.

summary: In this fireside chat, Gergely Orosz interviews Simon Eskildsen, CEO and co-founder of Turbopuffer, a vector and full-text search engine built on S3 object storage. Simon traces his computing origins from PowerPoint animations through PHP and competitive programming (IOI), to being recruited by Shopify after a viral Nokia phone article on Hacker News. At Shopify (2013-2021), he compensated for lacking formal CS education by noting every unfamiliar concept and studying it deeply that evening, gravitating toward infrastructure engineering during 120-140% annual growth. He tackled containerization, database sharding (cut-over a week before Black Friday), multi-datacenter expansion, and built Toxiproxy—a fault injection proxy for CI-based chaos testing. His napkin math project—a GitHub table of ~50 hardware performance numbers—provided a framework for computing theoretical performance ceilings from first principles, which he used to challenge benchmarks and investigate phenomena like f-sync batching. After leaving Shopify, angel engineering at Readwise exposed him to vector search cost problems: vector storage would cost $30K/month against their $5K/month infrastructure budget. This economic pressure led him to build Turbopuffer on S3, launching in October 2023 at $1 per million vectors versus ~$100 previously—a 100x cost reduction. Cursor became the first customer after Simon debugged their Postgres autovacuum issues and delivered a promised 95% bill reduction. The conversation also covers CPU scarcity driven by RL and AI agent workloads, a memorable Jensen Huang meeting at Nvidia, Simon's outsider approach to venture capital (raising $700K with an open-cards philosophy), and Turbopuffer's remote-first culture built on campfires, twice-yearly offsites, and turbo credits.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this video form a coherent narrative about building cost-efficient AI infrastructure from first principles. Napkin math provides the analytical foundation—computing theoretical performance ceilings from hardware numbers—that enabled Simon to identify the 100x cost mismatch between DRAM-based and S3-based vector storage. Object storage as a database backend, vector clustering, and P99 latency optimization represent the engineering response to that economic insight. Fault injection testing (Toxiproxy) and BPF tracing demonstrate the debugging and validation practices that ensure such systems are reliable. The AI concepts—vector search, embedding-based recommendations, RL compute demands, and CPU scarcity—provide the market context that made Turbopuffer necessary: ChatGPT's 2022 release created an explosion in vector search demand, while RL and AI agent workloads are simultaneously creating CPU scarcity that constrains all cloud infrastructure. Together, these concepts illustrate how first-principles engineering analysis, applied to an emerging AI infrastructure cost problem, can produce a 100x cost reduction while maintaining production-grade reliability.
temporalContext: Video published August 3, 2026 on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. Research conducted as of August 23, 2026. Simon Eskildsen was at Shopify 2013-2021, angel engineering 2021-2023, and co-founded Turbopuffer in October 2023. Turbopuffer's first customer (Cursor) joined when Cursor was approximately 8 people. The AWS Startups case study was published December 2025. ChatGPT's 2022 release is cited as the catalyst for recurring vector search problems. The conversation references the post-ChatGPT AI infrastructure landscape, including current RL-driven CPU scarcity across cloud providers as of mid-2026.

concepts.name: Vector search
concepts.explanation: Searching using high-dimensional vector embeddings rather than traditional keyword matching, enabling semantic similarity retrieval for applications like code search (Cursor) and recommendation systems (Readwise).
concepts.importance: The core AI capability that Turbopuffer serves; the post-ChatGPT explosion in vector search demand created the market opportunity that Simon identified through angel engineering.

concepts.name: Embedding-based recommendation systems
concepts.explanation: Using vector embeddings to power recommendation engines, demonstrated by Simon building a system at Readwise so effective it inferred a co-founder's wife was pregnant from reading patterns.
concepts.importance: Illustrates the power of embedding-based personalization and the infrastructure cost it imposes, which directly motivated Turbopuffer's S3-based architecture.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning compute demands
concepts.explanation: RL workloads consuming massive CPU resources, creating scarcity across cloud providers and shifting where new CPUs are deployed based on power availability rather than demand alone.
concepts.importance: Explains the macro-level infrastructure constraint that makes Turbopuffer's multi-SKU compute strategy a competitive advantage, and contextualizes the CPU scarcity affecting all cloud-based AI infrastructure.

concepts.name: CPU scarcity from AI workloads
concepts.explanation: AI agents and RL training creating severe CPU scarcity across cloud providers, with power infrastructure availability determining CPU allocation and even large companies fighting for allocations.
concepts.importance: A current infrastructure reality that shapes cloud strategy for AI companies; Turbopuffer mitigates this by running flexibly across many machine SKUs (C4, C4A ARM, Z4D) rather than requiring specific instance types.

concepts.name: AVX 512 and SIMD for vector processing
concepts.explanation: Advanced CPU instruction sets (AVX 512, SIMD) that enable efficient vector computation, central to Turbopuffer's CPU-centric strategy and Simon's enthusiastic advocacy at Nvidia despite being warned not to mention CPUs.
concepts.importance: Highlights that vector search can be performed efficiently on CPUs using specialized instruction sets, challenging the assumption that GPU acceleration is always necessary for AI workloads.

concepts.name: Vector search cost economics
concepts.explanation: The economic mismatch between DRAM-based vector storage (~$100 per million vectors) and S3-based storage ($1 per million), driven by the approximately 100x cost difference between memory (~$2/GB/month) and S3 (~$0.02/GB/month).
concepts.importance: The fundamental economic insight that created Turbopuffer's market opportunity; extreme cost mismatches in infrastructure signal opportunities for architectural innovation.

concepts.name: Napkin math methodology
concepts.explanation: A framework of approximately 50 hardware performance numbers (DRAM bandwidth, S3 roundtrip costs, NVMe SSD bandwidth, per-gigabyte costs) maintained on GitHub, used to compute theoretical performance ceilings from first principles and challenge benchmark claims by comparing actual performance against computed limits.
concepts.importance: Central analytical tool that enabled Simon to identify the 100x cost mismatch between DRAM and S3 vector storage, investigate f-sync batching in MySQL, and make pricing commitments to Cursor based on rough calculations.

concepts.name: Database sharding
concepts.explanation: Splitting a large database into smaller horizontal partitions to handle scale, demonstrated by Shopify executing a sharding cut-over one week before Black Friday during 120-140% year-over-year growth.
concepts.importance: Illustrates the high-stakes infrastructure decisions required during hypergrowth and the operational discipline needed to execute risky migrations under tight deadlines.

concepts.name: Fault injection testing (Toxiproxy)
concepts.explanation: A layer 4/7 TCP proxy that sits between applications and databases, enabling API-driven injection of failures (downtime, latency, corruption) in CI environments to systematically validate failure handling. Called 'Toxyroxy' in the transcript; actual project name is Toxiproxy.
concepts.importance: Uncovered tens of issues in MySQL drivers and Rails failure handling at Shopify, demonstrating how proxy-based chaos testing in CI catches real driver-level bugs that mocking cannot.

concepts.name: F-sync batching
concepts.explanation: Databases batch f-sync operations on 4K blocks, enabling write throughput (10,000 writes/s) far exceeding the naive f-sync-per-write calculation (~1,000 writes/s at 1ms per f-sync). Discovered through BPF tracing investigation.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how napkin math can identify discrepancies between theoretical and actual performance, leading to deep system-level discoveries that improve infrastructure understanding.

concepts.name: Object storage as database backend
concepts.explanation: Using S3 object storage as the durable source of truth for a database rather than DRAM, trading higher per-request latency (~200ms P99) for dramatically lower cost (~100x cheaper per GB), with multi-tier caching to mitigate round-trip latency.
concepts.importance: Core architectural innovation behind Turbopuffer that enabled a 100x cost reduction in vector storage, fundamentally challenging the assumption that vector search requires DRAM.

concepts.name: Vector clustering and centroid-based search
concepts.explanation: Clustering vectors into files stored in S3 with a centroid IDs file, downloading centroids first then the N closest clusters for search, minimizing data transfer from object storage and bounding the number of round trips.
concepts.importance: The initial algorithmic approach that made S3-based vector search feasible despite high per-request latency, by reducing the number of sequential S3 requests per query.

concepts.name: P99/P999 latency optimization
concepts.explanation: Optimizing for tail latency across multiple sequential S3 round trips, where P99 latency (~200ms per 256-512KB object) compounds across each tree-traversal step in a vector search query.
concepts.importance: Critical for user-facing search systems where tail latency determines perceived performance; minimizing round trips is the primary lever for acceptable query times on object storage.

concepts.name: GDB-based fault simulation
concepts.explanation: Attaching GDB to a running process and closing its database file descriptor to simulate a database failure and observe application degradation behavior, a manual technique used before building the automated Toxiproxy tool.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how low-level debugging tools can be repurposed for reliability testing, and how manual fault simulation motivated building systematic CI-integrated alternatives.

concepts.name: BPF tracing for system investigation
concepts.explanation: Using BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) to trace system calls at the kernel level, used by Simon to discover f-sync batching behavior in MySQL before LLMs made research easier.
concepts.importance: Illustrates deep-system investigation techniques that reveal non-obvious performance behaviors, and how kernel-level tracing can validate or refute napkin math predictions.

concepts.name: Multi-tier cache hierarchy
concepts.explanation: Evolution from nginx reverse proxy caching to direct file-based caching (Justine's first contribution), and later to a multi-tier hierarchy (object storage to NVMe SSD to memory) to serve queries efficiently while maintaining S3 as source of truth.
concepts.importance: Shows how caching strategy evolves from quick MVP solutions to production-grade architectures, and how each tier addresses different latency and cost trade-offs.

concepts.name: Self-education through systematic concept note-taking
concepts.explanation: A learning method of noting every unfamiliar concept encountered at work on a piece of paper and studying each deeply that evening, compensating for lack of formal CS education.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates a practical and transferable self-education strategy that enabled Simon to rapidly close knowledge gaps in a high-growth engineering environment.

concepts.name: Simplicity as a core engineering principle
concepts.explanation: Shipping the simplest possible MVP to validate market demand before investing in production-grade infrastructure, informed by long tenures where simplicity proved to win as software ages.
concepts.importance: Turbopuffer launched with a single GCP instance and nginx caching despite not being a proper HA setup, yet validated demand and earned trust through reliability of S3-committed writes.

concepts.name: Infrastructure scaling at hypergrowth
concepts.explanation: Managing infrastructure during 120-140% year-over-year growth including Docker containerization, multi-datacenter expansion, decomposing a 128GB Redis server, and Black Friday capacity planning with months-ahead commitments.
concepts.importance: Provides real-world context for the infrastructure engineering skills that later informed Turbopuffer's design, and illustrates the operational pressures of scaling during hypergrowth.

concepts.name: Venture capital decision framework
concepts.explanation: A six-reason model for evaluating when to raise capital (R&D, growth, founder ego, employee liquidity, strategic partnerships, M&A) with explicit warnings that ego-driven raises dilute all employees and set artificial price ceilings.
concepts.importance: Provides a structured decision framework for founders evaluating fundraising, grounded in Simon's experience raising $700K with an open-cards approach that terrified some VCs.

concepts.name: Remote-first engineering culture
concepts.explanation: Distributed company practices including spontaneous 'campfire' gatherings where anyone can join, twice-yearly offsites, and 'turbo credits' that reward extracurricular contributions (conference talks, blog posts) with flight upgrades to business class.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates a novel approach to remote culture for an infrastructure company, combining structured offsites with spontaneous in-person gatherings and creative incentive systems.

sections.title: Early computing history: PowerPoint to PHP
sections.summary: Simon describes his introduction to computers through PowerPoint's touring-complete animation capabilities, then FrontPage web development, HTML exploration, PHP, and Dreamweaver. He exhausted Danish-language programming resources around age 11-12, then spent four years addicted to World of Warcraft, which dramatically improved his English.

sections.title: International Olympiad in Informatics and competitive programming
sections.summary: An Australian internet friend introduced Simon to the International Olympiad in Informatics. He found the Danish team application and began solving algorithmic problems very different from his web development background, such as NP-complete optimization scenarios.

sections.title: Shopify recruitment during high school
sections.summary: Simon wrote an article about switching from an iPhone to a Nokia brick phone in 2013, which went viral on Hacker News and was featured in the New York Times. A Shopify recruiter connected him to the Ottawa office. He interviewed, revealed he was still in high school, finished school, then relocated to Canada in 2013.

sections.title: Self-education and deep learning at Shopify
sections.summary: Initially insecure about lacking formal CS education, Simon adopted a method of noting every unfamiliar concept mentioned by colleagues and studying each deeply that evening. This compulsion to peel back layers drew him toward infrastructure engineering, sitting with the team closest to the metal at lunch.

sections.title: Infrastructure scaling challenges at Shopify
sections.summary: Simon describes Shopify's 120-140% year-over-year growth, annual Black Friday preparation, Docker containerization, database sharding (cut-over a week before Black Friday), multi-datacenter expansion, decomposing a 128GB Redis server, and building failure-mode matrices. He used GDB to close database file descriptors in running processes to simulate failures.

sections.title: Toxyroxy: CI-based fault injection proxy
sections.summary: Simon created Toxyroxy, a layer 4/7 proxy sitting between applications and databases, enabling API calls to simulate database failures, slowness, and data corruption in CI. This uncovered tens of issues in MySQL drivers and Rails failure handling. Toxyroxy is still running in Shopify's CI system.

sections.title: Decision to leave Shopify after eight years
sections.summary: After eight years at Shopify (2013-2021), Simon wanted novelty and exposure to different companies. He and co-founder Justine wrote Shopify's storefront, which powered almost 100% of traffic 18 months after they started. Simon left without knowing exactly what he wanted to do next.

sections.title: Napkin math project: challenging poor benchmarks
sections.summary: Simon's napkin math project is a GitHub table of ~50 performance numbers (DRAM bandwidth, S3 roundtrip costs, NVMe SSD bandwidth, EBS volume bandwidth, per-gigabyte costs) with an R script and flash cards. He used it to challenge infrastructure decisions based on poor benchmarks, computing theoretical performance from first principles.

sections.title: F-sync investigation and batching discovery
sections.summary: Simon hypothesized that MySQL writes per second should equal f-syncs per second (~1,000 at 1ms each), but found MySQL achieves 10,000 writes per second on a modest box. Using BPF tracing (pre-LLM, so research took a long time), he discovered f-sync batching on 4K blocks.

sections.title: Three ingredients converging into Turbopuffer
sections.summary: Three factors converged: (1) a frustrating experience with a traditional search database at Shopify that never matched napkin math predictions, (2) the napkin math project giving him facility with theoretical performance ceilings, and (3) angel engineering at friends' companies where vector search problems kept recurring after ChatGPT's 2022 release.

sections.title: Readwise: the cost problem that sparked Turbopuffer
sections.summary: While angel engineering at Readwise, a bootstrapped Canadian company spending ~$5K/month on infrastructure, Simon built a recommendation engine so effective it inferred a co-founder's wife was pregnant from reading patterns. Back-of-envelope math showed vector storage would cost $30K/month—six times their entire infrastructure budget—so they didn't ship it. This cost mismatch drove Simon to ask whether vectors could be stored in S3 instead of DRAM.

sections.title: Building Turbopuffer on S3: summer 2023
sections.summary: Simon spent summer 2023 iterating on approaches to overcome S3's ~200ms P99 latency, which compounds across tree-traversal round trips. He optimized for P99/P999 because each query involves multiple S3 requests. A first working prototype emerged in July 2023. After two rewrites, he released in October 2023. The initial version used simple clustering—vectors clustered into files named cluster1/2/3 in S3 with a centroidids file—and an nginx reverse proxy for caching, running on a single 8-core GCP instance.

sections.title: Launching on Twitter and Cursor as first customer
sections.summary: Simon launched Turbopuffer on Twitter at $1 per million vectors versus ~$100 previously, knowing the system was reliable (all writes committed to S3, no data loss on VM shutdown) despite being the simplest possible version. Cursor, then ~8 people, reached out after struggling with DRAM-based vector unit economics. They had tried Postgres and AWS Aurora without success. Simon flew to San Francisco, helped debug their Postgres autovacuum issues, and built trust. Co-founder Justine, whom Simon considered the best engineer at Shopify, joined the project.

sections.title: Justine's improvements and Cursor migration
sections.summary: Justine's first contribution was replacing the nginx reverse proxy cache with a direct file-based cache. Cursor migrated everything over within 1-2 weeks. Simon had promised to reduce their bill by 95% and delivered—Cursor's first Turbopuffer bill was 95% lower than their previous Aurora bill. Cursor's leadership acknowledged you should never bet your business on a tiny startup as your biggest customer, except for Turbopuffer.

sections.title: Meeting Jensen Huang at Nvidia
sections.summary: At an Nvidia event with Jensen Huang and ~50 Nvidia leadership members present, Simon opened with a joke about Turbopuffer being able to pivot into vapes if things went south. Jensen replied, 'Judging by your slide, maybe you should.' Simon then asked Jensen if he vapes. Despite being warned by his team not to mention CPUs, Simon couldn't stop praising AVX 512, SIMD, and CPU availability, stopping just short of saying he was glad not to need GPUs.

sections.title: CPU scarcity and cloud capacity competition
sections.summary: Simon explains that RL workloads and AI agents are consuming massive CPU resources, creating scarcity across cloud providers. Power availability determines where new CPUs ship. Even large companies fight for allocations. Turbopuffer mitigates this by running flexibly across many machine SKUs—favoring C4s and ARM C4As on GCP, and Z4Ds—rather than requiring specific instance types. Simon notes that at Shopify, he had to commit capacity months ahead of Black Friday, illustrating clouds are not infinite.

sections.title: Venture capital philosophy and the six reasons to raise
sections.summary: Simon approached venture capital as a self-described 'outsider squared'—from Denmark to Ottawa to San Francisco—initially unsure whether Turbopuffer could be a billion-dollar company. He and Justine went six months without salary, spending tens of thousands on GCP bills. Wanting to hire Buen (Boyan), a former IOI competitor from North Macedonia, Simon called a Silicon Valley contact named Locky to raise $700K for two engineers. He told VCs he would shut down and return everything if no PMF by year-end—an open-cards approach that terrified some VCs and was perceived as low ambition on the West Coast. They raised, hired Buen and Morgan, and became profitable later that year. Simon identifies six reasons to raise capital: (1) R&D, (2) growth, (3) founder ego, (4) employee liquidity, (5) strategic partnerships, (6) M&A. He warns that ego-driven raises are dangerous because they dilute all employees and set artificial price ceilings for future hires. Turbopuffer's first raise was for R&D, the second for employee liquidity.

sections.title: Remote-first culture: campfires and turbo credits
sections.summary: Simon explains Turbopuffer's fully remote culture, which started in 2023 on the cusp of COVID. He notes only two cities—San Francisco and maybe New York—can build a database company fast, so going remote required going all-in on a distributed model. The company gathers everyone twice yearly for offsites (e.g., Mexico City). The 'campfire' concept encourages spontaneous gatherings: when a few people congregate somewhere, anyone can join for customer meetings and dinners. Some employees attend only offsites; others travel every two weeks. Turbo credits reward extracurricular contributions (conference talks, blog posts, expo-floor work) with flight upgrades to business class, encouraging in-person collaboration. Employees are already joking about creating a central bank and betting market for turbo credits. Gergely closes by observing the conversation focused on engineering principles, curiosity, and human connection rather than AI itself.

organization.name: Turbopuffer Inc.
organization.summary: Turbopuffer Inc. is a Canadian technology company founded on October 4, 2023, by Simon Hørup Eskildsen (co-founder & CEO) and Justine Li (co-founder), both formerly of Shopify where they scaled infrastructure from 1K to 1M RPS over 8 years. Headquartered in Ottawa, Ontario, with additional offices in Vancouver and New York City, Turbopuffer builds a serverless vector and full-text search engine on object storage (S3/GCS), achieving approximately 10x cost reduction versus memory-based alternatives. The company crossed $100M ARR in March 2026, is profitable, and has raised less than $1M total from Lachy Groom and Thrive Capital. As of mid-2026, the company has approximately 37 employees distributed across 6 countries, hosting 1T+ documents with 10M+ writes/s and 25k+ queries/s. Notable customers include Cursor, Anthropic, Notion, Cognition, Harvey, Bridgewater, Ramp, Linear, Legora, Superhuman, Atlassian, and Granola.

technologies.label: Turbopuffer — Object-storage-based vector search
technologies.summary: Turbopuffer is a vector and full-text search engine built on S3 object storage, achieving a 100x cost reduction ($1 vs ~$100 per million vectors) by using S3 as the durable source of truth rather than DRAM. The architecture uses SPFresh centroid-based ANN indexing to minimize object storage round-trips, with a multi-tier cache hierarchy (object storage → NVMe SSD → memory) to mitigate S3's ~200ms P99 latency. Simon launched in October 2023 after iterating through summer 2023 and two rewrites; Cursor became the first customer after Simon debugged their Postgres autovacuum issues and delivered a promised 95% bill reduction. The company runs flexibly across many cloud machine SKUs (C4, C4A ARM, Z4D) to mitigate CPU scarcity driven by RL and AI agent workloads.
technologies.role: Primary subject of the interview; Simon describes the founding story, architecture, cost economics, customer acquisition journey, and current scale of Turbopuffer.

technologies.label: Napkin math — First-principles performance estimation
technologies.summary: Napkin math is a methodology for estimating system performance from first-principles hardware numbers. Simon maintains a GitHub repository with approximately 50 key performance numbers (DRAM bandwidth ~100 GB/s, S3 P99 latency ~200ms, NVMe SSD bandwidth, per-GB costs: memory ~$2/GB/month vs S3 ~$0.02/GB/month) used to compute theoretical performance ceilings and challenge benchmark claims. This methodology enabled the discovery of f-sync batching in MySQL (where 10,000 writes/s exceeded the naive 1,000/s calculation from 1ms per f-sync) through BPF tracing investigation, and was critical to identifying the 100x cost mismatch between DRAM-based and S3-based vector storage that motivated Turbopuffer.
technologies.role: Central analytical framework; Simon describes using napkin math to challenge benchmarks at Shopify, investigate f-sync behavior in MySQL, identify the DRAM vs S3 cost mismatch at Readwise, and make pricing commitments to Cursor.

technologies.label: Toxiproxy — CI-based fault injection proxy
technologies.summary: Toxiproxy (called 'Toxyroxy' in the transcript) is a layer 4/7 TCP proxy created by Simon at Shopify that sits between applications and databases, enabling API-driven injection of failures (downtime, latency, data corruption) in CI environments. It evolved from Simon's manual technique of using GDB to attach to running processes and close database file descriptors to simulate failures. Toxiproxy uncovered tens of issues in MySQL drivers and Rails failure handling at Shopify, and remains in use in Shopify's CI system since October 2014. The tool is written in Go with an HTTP API on port 8474.
technologies.role: Described as a key engineering achievement during Simon's Shopify tenure (2013-2021), illustrating the evolution from manual fault simulation to systematic CI-integrated chaos testing that uncovered real driver-level bugs.

prerequisites: Understanding of database internals including f-sync, B-trees, query planning, and autovacuum
Knowledge of S3/object storage latency characteristics and access patterns
Understanding of vector search and embedding-based recommendation systems
Familiarity with CPU instruction sets such as AVX 512 and SIMD, and cloud instance types
Knowledge of reinforcement learning compute requirements and cloud capacity dynamics
Familiarity with venture capital terminology including PMF, dilution, and liquidity
Basic understanding of distributed systems caching and multi-tier cache hierarchies
Familiarity with CI/CD pipelines and integration testing concepts
outcomes: Apply napkin math methodology to compute theoretical performance ceilings from first-principles hardware numbers and challenge benchmark claims
Design fault injection test suites using proxy-based approaches (Toxiproxy pattern) to systematically validate failure handling in CI
Explain how f-sync batching on 4K blocks enables databases to achieve write throughput far exceeding naive f-sync-per-write calculations
Analyze the trade-offs of building a vector search engine on object storage (S3) versus DRAM, including latency compounding across round trips
Identify extreme cost mismatches in infrastructure as signals for architectural innovation, using the Readwise $30K/month vs $5K/month case as a model
Evaluate angel engineering as an alternative to passive angel investing for gaining market exposure and identifying recurring problems
Assess hands-on technical support as a trust-building strategy in B2B infrastructure sales, using the Cursor Postgres debugging narrative
Analyze how reinforcement learning and AI agent workloads create CPU scarcity and the implications for multi-cloud SKU strategy
Evaluate simplicity as a core engineering principle and its long-term impact on software maintainability and operational complexity
Analyze venture capital decisions through a framework of six reasons to raise capital, identifying ego-driven dilution risks
Design remote-first engineering culture practices including campfire gatherings, structured offsites, and creative incentive systems
challengeSeeds: Given DRAM bandwidth (~100GB/s), S3 P99 latency (~200ms for 256-512KB objects), and NVMe SSD bandwidth, estimate the theoretical P99 latency for a vector search query traversing a 3-level centroid tree on S3. Compare your estimate against Turbopuffer's published 200ms P99 claim and explain any discrepancies.

Design a fault injection test suite using a Toxiproxy-style proxy for an application with MySQL and Redis dependencies. Specify which failure modes to inject (downtime, latency, corruption), what application behaviors to validate, and how to integrate these tests into a CI pipeline.

Calculate the cost-per-million-vectors for DRAM-based versus S3-based vector storage using napkin math pricing (memory ~$2/GB/month, S3 ~$0.02/GB/month). Assume 1KB per vector embedding. Identify the break-even point and explain why Turbopuffer achieved a 100x cost reduction.

Using napkin math, estimate MySQL write throughput assuming f-sync batching on 4K blocks. Explain why the naive calculation (1 f-sync/ms = 1,000 writes/s) underestimates actual throughput (~10,000 writes/s), and describe how BPF tracing could be used to verify the batching behavior.

Propose a multi-cloud compute strategy for a vector search service facing CPU scarcity driven by RL workloads. Justify your choice of machine SKUs across GCP (C4, C4A ARM, Z4D) and AWS, and explain how SKU flexibility mitigates capacity allocation risk.
